claims.claim: Sync workers hold one request each while they wait, so in-flight requests need about one worker each (120–360 workers at 600 req/s, roughly 7–21 times today's fleet)
claims.measured: python-flask I/O-wait (10 ms wait, 256 connections): 276 req/s, p50 915 ms, CPU 18%, against 1,732 req/s on plaintext
claims.why: Sync Flask's throughput drops more than 6x when each request waits, while CPU sits at 18%, so it is limited by worker count, as the answer says.

claims.claim: Switching to gevent workers is the way to handle a long insurer wait without rewriting, instead of staying on sync workers
claims.measured: I/O wait: python-flask-gevent 2,956 req/s vs python-flask 276 req/s (about 10.7x); p50 71 ms vs 915 ms
claims.why: Gevent served about 10x more waiting requests than sync Flask on one CPU, so recommending it for I/O-bound waits matches the data.

claims.claim: Threaded workers (gthread) give much smaller headroom than gevent because thread counts per process stay low
claims.measured: I/O wait: python-flask-gthread 374 req/s (CPU 19%) vs python-flask-gevent 2,956 req/s (CPU 99%)
claims.why: Gthread reached only about 1/8 of gevent's throughput under I/O wait and left the CPU mostly idle, which fits 'much smaller headroom'.

claims.claim: Running 300+ sync worker processes means you should check per-process memory across that many processes
claims.measured: python-flask peak memory 122 MB and idle 115 MB per container; per-worker memory is not measured
claims.why: The measurements give memory per container, not per worker process, so the memory cost of scaling to hundreds of workers can't be checked.
